sentences.text: Dakosaurus was an extinct genus of crocodylomorph belonging to the family Metriorhynchidae.
All known species were large animals, reaching about 4 to 5 meters in length with skulls and jaws up to 1 meter long, featuring serrated edges and laterally compressed teeth.
The animal possessed a streamlined body and a tail with a large fin, making it a more efficient swimmer than modern crocodilians.
Its triangular skull contained large openings that housed strong muscles for a powerful bite, anchored by large abductor muscles in the supratemporal fenestrae.
Although its limbs were reduced, the femur remained robust, measuring 32 cm in one specimen and 43 cm in the neotype.
The species D. andiniensis has a unique short, tall snout that earned it the nickname 'Godzilla' in press reports.
Dakosaurus was the only marine crocodiliform to evolve both laterally compressed and serrated teeth, which were larger than those of any other metriorhynchid.
A 2026 study reported cartilaginous fish remains found within the abdominal region of a new D. maximus specimen.
The teeth interlocked like those of gharials and killer whales when the jaws were closed.
The genus was established by Friedrich August von Quenstedt in 1856 based on an isolated tooth previously named Geosaurus maximus by Plieninger.
Early isolated teeth of Dakosaurus were initially mistaken for belonging to the dinosaur Megalosaurus.
Dacosaurus and Megalosaurus schnaitheimi are listed as synonyms for Dakosaurus.

Wear on the teeth suggests they ground against each other to shear flesh, indicating a macrocarnivorous diet, and the animal was likely capable of feeding by twisting to tear chunks of meat from its prey.
Dakosaurus and Geosaurus giganteus were likely top predators in the Solnhofen limestone ecosystem, both possessing large short-snouted skulls and serrated teeth.
It is hypothesized that niche partitioning allowed multiple crocodyliform species to coexist.
The type species of the genus is Geosaurus maximus.
The parent group of Dakosaurus is Dakosaurina.
A 2012 study reclassified D. manselii into the genus Plesiosuchus to resolve issues with the paraphyletic nature of Dakosaurus.
Dakosaurus fossils range from the Oxfordian to the Berriasian stages.
Fossils of Dakosaurus have been found in Late Jurassic deposits across England, France, Switzerland, Germany, Poland, Russia, Argentina, and Mexico.
Dakosaurus was a carnivore that spent most, if not all, of its life in the sea.
It is debated whether Dakosaurus gave birth in the water like dolphins and ichthyosaurs or laid eggs on the coast like turtles, as no eggs or nests are known.
